# Results — Study 456 (Belt-Hold / opening marubozu)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a bullish
belt-hold (opens at its low, no lower wick; closes well up; after a downtrend) reverses the
move** — encoded as a mechanical rule. The flag is read on the close of t (white body, open at
the low, tall body, prior downtrend); a long fires on the belt-hold close, entered at the **next
close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **666** mechanical bullish belt-holds pooled across the 5 tapes (wick ≤ 10% of range, body ≥ 60% of range, 10-bar prior downtrend) |
| Timing / costs | belt-hold read on the close of t; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per signal |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument candlestick study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects
> only the drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — belt-hold vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch belt-hold-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = belt-hold − random.

| horizon | n | belt-hold | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (bh−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 665 | +31.8 bps | 59% | +2.36 | +33.4 bps | **−1.7 bps** | +29.8 bps | −0.11 | 0.909 |
| 10-day | 665 | +66.5 bps | 62% | +3.71 | +57.2 bps | **+9.3 bps** | +64.5 bps | +0.47 | 0.635 |
| 20-day | 665 | +104.6 bps | 67% | +3.68 | +71.9 bps | **+32.8 bps** | +102.6 bps | +1.15 | 0.251 |
| 60-day | 660 | +306.0 bps | 69% | +5.86 | +212.1 bps | **+93.9 bps** | +304.0 bps | **+2.03** | 0.042 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks strong (**+3.68** at 20 days, **+5.86**
at 60) — but that is mostly **beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index inherit the
drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the belt-hold is a coin-flip at 5/10/20
days (Δ = −1.7 / +9.3 / +32.8 bps; Welch *t* never reaches 1.2) and only **marginally** beats
random at 60 days (+93.9 bps, Welch *t* = +2.03, *p* = 0.042). That single long-horizon, just-over-the-bar
result is the only thing standing between this rule and a clean "nothing there" — and the placebo
below shows it isn't the candle shape doing it.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent cross-sectional edge

| ticker | entries | belt-hold | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (bh−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 121 | +119.5 bps | +2.49 | +22.4 bps | **+97.2 bps** |
| QQQ | 139 | +126.6 bps | +1.55 | +160.1 bps | **−33.5 bps** |
| IWM | 126 | +67.0 bps | +1.04 | +29.2 bps | **+37.8 bps** |
| DIA | 137 | +89.8 bps | +1.48 | +62.6 bps | **+27.3 bps** |
| GLD | 143 | +118.1 bps | +2.56 | +74.7 bps | **+43.4 bps** |

The 20-day delta is positive in 4 of 5 names, but driven almost entirely by **SPY** (+97 bps) and
flips **negative** on QQQ (−34 bps). No single-name one-sample *t* clears 2 except GLD (+2.56, a
non-equity tape). The pattern is a scattered, name-dependent tilt — not the uniform reversal the
folklore promises.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the candle shape, nothing changes

The decisive "does the open-at-low geometry matter?" test: keep the **prior-downtrend** filter
and the **signal count**, but draw the entries from random downtrend bars — throwing away the
belt-hold candle shape while preserving the marginal. If price genuinely reverses because the
**open sat at the extreme**, the shape-blind draws should rarely match the real result.

| test | observed belt-hold 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shape-scramble | +119.5 bps | **0.433** | 500 |

**43% of shape-scrambled draws (random downtrend bars) match or beat the real belt-hold**
(*p* = 0.433). The open-at-the-low geometry carries no extra information over "just buy *some* bar
in a downtrend." The candle shape is not load-bearing — what little edge exists is the
prior-downtrend context (a slow mean-reversion / drift mix), not the belt-hold itself.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real reversal

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* belt-hold reversal (knob `edge`), the same rule behaves
exactly as it must — so the flat/marginal real-tape result is a genuine reading, not a dead
detector.

| planted edge | n | belt-hold | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no reversal) | 200 | +11.5 bps | 48% | +0.27 |
| **0.40** (real planted reversal) | 140 | +955.8 bps | 92% | **+13.14** |

With no planted reversal the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted reversal
lights up at *t* = +13.14 with a 92% win-rate. The detector is live and sensitive.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The belt-hold is a coin-flip vs a drift-matched random baseline at 5/10/20
  days (Δ = −1.7 / +9.3 / +32.8 bps; Welch *t* ≤ 1.15) and only **marginally** beats random at
  60 days (Δ = +93.9 bps, Welch *t* = +2.03, *p* = 0.042). One of four horizons, barely over the
  bar, concentrated in a single name (SPY) — enough to deny a clean "None", far short of a
  robust "Real". The big one-sample *t*'s (20-day +3.68, 60-day +5.86) are mostly beta.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Whatever edge exists shows up only at the longest horizon, leans on
  one instrument, and survives costs only because it is so slow (one 60-day hold). It is the
  prior-downtrend / drift context, not a deployable candlestick signal. Nothing robust to scale.
- **"Does the opening-at-extreme reverse"? — BUSTED.** The shape-scramble placebo leaves the
  result intact (*p* = 0.433): random downtrend bars do as well as the real belt-hold, so the
  open-at-the-low geometry carries no forecasting information. The marginal 60-day edge is the
  downtrend context, not the candle. The belt-hold is a descriptive label, not a reversal signal.
